<reason>Side B (PRO) built the stronger path to victory by establishing a decisive burden: a healthy corrective must remain correctable itself. Side B effectively argued that populism's defining claim to exclusively embody "the people" inherently delegitimizes checks, losers' consent, and independent referees—closing the very exits (courts, media, elections) that allow citizens to punish bad governments. While Side A (CON) persuasively argued that populism responds to genuine elite capture and can force accountability, it failed to fully neutralize the objection that populist methods destroy the epistemic and institutional infrastructure needed for democratic correction. Side B's distinction between "flawed-but-competitive" elite capture (which preserves plural points of attack) and populist capture (which systematically closes them) proved decisive on the "usually" prong of the proposition. Side B also delivered sharper rebuttals, particularly the "loyalty test" critique showing that populist legitimacy becomes conditional on outcome rather than procedure.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's Rebuttal 2 (Turn 7), where B answered Side A's pressure question about the captured baseline by arguing that populist rule is worse than competitive elite capture because it eliminates the capacity for future correction—transforming multiple veto points into a single point of failure controlled by the leader.</best_rebuttal>
